reading.title: How Headlines Shape What Readers See
reading.purpose: Examine how word choice and missing facts can tilt news coverage of a debate.
paras: Suppose a city council debates a controversial proposal to replace two street parking lanes with a bus-only lane. Because drivers, shop owners, and bus riders strongly disagree, the same meeting can produce very different news stories. A reader's perception—the way a person sees and understands an event—often depends on which headline appears first on a screen.

Every writer has a point of view, yet honest reporters work hard to keep a clear slant from taking over the facts. A partisan blogger, fiercely loyal to one side and unfair to the other, does the opposite. Driven by a clear agenda, a goal the writer wants to advance, that blogger may choose only quotes that make opponents look foolish. Such selective reporting leaves readers seeing half a picture while believing they saw it all.

One of the easiest ways to skew a story is not to invent a lie, but simply to omit key details. Imagine a report that mentions higher construction costs while leaving out the number of commuters who will reach work faster. Even a chart can manipulate an audience if the bars start at ninety instead of zero, making a tiny gap look like a cliff. When loyalty or allegiance to a favorite team or party comes before accuracy, facts bend to fit the slogan.

How can readers protect themselves? Start by comparing at least two sources on the same topic. Ask what evidence is quoted, what facts are missing, and who benefits if you agree. Recognizing bias does not mean trusting nothing; it means checking the frame before accepting the picture.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "partisan" most nearly means
choices: carefully checking two independent sources before publishing
fiercely loyal to one side while treating others unfairly
willing to change a headline after a city council vote
focused mainly on local bus schedules and road repairs
qs.why: Paragraph 2 defines partisan directly as "fiercely loyal to one side and unfair to the other."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how a graph can mislead readers without using false numbers?
choices: One of the easiest ways to skew a story is not to invent a lie, but simply to omit key details.
Imagine a report that mentions higher construction costs while leaving out the number of commuters who will reach work faster.
Even a chart can manipulate an audience if the bars start at ninety instead of zero, making a tiny gap look like a cliff.
When loyalty or allegiance to a favorite team or party comes before accuracy, facts bend to fit the slogan.
qs.why: This sentence explains how starting a chart's axis at ninety instead of zero exaggerates a tiny difference.

ev.text: Even a chart can manipulate an audience if the bars start at ninety instead of zero, making a tiny gap look like a cliff.

qs.q: Why does the author advise comparing at least two sources on the same topic?
choices: Seeing two accounts helps readers notice missing details and one-sided framing.
Every news organization makes up completely fake numbers about city projects.
Most readers prefer reading two short headlines instead of one full article.
City council meetings are usually closed to reporters who write for local papers.
qs.why: Because a single biased report can omit facts or skew charts, comparing sources reveals what was left out.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Bus-only lanes always hurt shop owners more than they help daily commuters.
News coverage can be tilted by selective facts and framing, so readers should check multiple sources.
Blogs should be banned from covering city council votes because bloggers have strong opinions.
Charts and graphs are too confusing for most readers to understand without a reporter's help.
qs.why: The reading explains how slant, agendas, omission, and misleading charts shape perception, and ends with habits for checking sources.
